toc.title: Change the state to change the story
Why I don't start with the thoughts

blocks.p: How do you deal with anger, and with being stuck in defensive thought patterns? I want to come at this from a different angle, using the concepts of the Polyvagal Theory and building from there. I hope it gives you a different way of looking at what anger is, what purpose it may serve, and how to shift out of it.

This came from a listener. I had asked, "What's your number one challenge?" and one person answered: "How to deal with being stuck in anger and defensive thought patterns, keeping a person in a state of anger." That's all they sent, nothing about their life, so this is very general.
Anger is the felt emotional experience of the fight sympathetic state of the autonomic nervous system.

That's different from someone who is actually in a fight state because they need to defend themselves and be aggressive. If you're in that state as a means of survival, in a situation where you have to be aggressive, you won't exactly feel it as anger. You'll probably feel it as power, and you'll be able to act on it.

Anger is when you have that fight flavoring in your system, but it hasn't been used. It's just kind of there, lingering. Maybe nothing is quite setting it off, so you generally feel it as irritation, maybe a low-level anger. Then something happens, and you do feel it as anger, and you come across as more dominant or aggressive.

When that state is lingering in your system, anger and irritability will be the most noticeable. You may also feel aggressive impulses, like taking up space or raising your voice. You might speak more quickly, in a rushed, monotone kind of voice, without the vocal prosody, that singsongy quality your voice has when you're in your safety state.
That lingering fight energy brings emotions like anger and irritability, and it also shifts your cognitions. The fight state flavors the thoughts in your mind.

You may know Deb Dana's concept of story follows state: whatever state you're in, your thoughts follow. The aggressive or blaming thoughts in your mind aren't there for no reason. You don't just have angry thoughts. They follow the state of your autonomic nervous system. If your nervous system is in more of a fight state, your thoughts will follow, and they'll be more blaming.

Deb Dana put it this way when I interviewed her: "You can see how the story changes dependent on the state, not depending on what I choose to think." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))
Here's a simple example. Ray is doing his homework at a local coffee shop, and he notices someone looking at him. Same scenario, but Ray's thoughts will be different depending on his state.

ul: Shutdown: "They see me and think I'm weird. I need to hide." He looks down and pulls his hoodie over his head.
Fight: "What the... are they looking at?" He might even grimace at the person, tensely.
Flight: "Well, shit, is there something on my face?" He hurriedly brushes at his face, or even goes to the bathroom to check.
Safety: "They're staring off into the distance. I like to zone out." He might even wave at them and share a laugh.

blocks.h: Change the state to change the story

blocks.p: So how does someone actually change their thoughts, and what does that have to do with their polyvagal state? If story follows state, then you need to change the state in order to change the story.

You can reframe your thoughts to change your state, and that can be helpful. But what I'm talking about here is directly addressing the stuck state itself, so your thoughts naturally change as a result. I think that's more helpful for the overall process of self-regulation and building distress tolerance than constantly trying to change the way you think, which can be more frustrating than anything for many of us.
To deal with being stuck in anger, you need to work with the body's state, which means allowing yourself to feel the fight state. You may need to allow yourself to feel some or all of that power.

That could absolutely be overwhelming. But as you build your capacity to sit with your feelings, to increase your distress tolerance, to increase the strength of your vagal brake, sitting with your stuck defensive state becomes possible: the emotions, the cognitions, the sensations, and the impulses within it.

It's possible to mindfully experience your stuck defensive state, or in this case to feel your fight state, and to allow the anger to be present. When you allow anger to be present, you're really allowing the fight state to exist. You're giving it permission.

We don't want to do this if you can't tolerate it. If you don't have the distress tolerance, you don't want to allow the anger to be there. You have to be able to handle it. Until you can address the stuck state itself, something else, like a simple coping skill or something to distract yourself, could be useful.

Allowing it isn't easy either, because to do that, you have to be anchored in your safety state first. Once you're anchored, you can be more curious about what's happening within. You can allow it to be present, maybe normalize it or validate that you have a feeling in the first place, and then get curious and ask, "What does it feel like? What's the actual experience of having this?" Then you get to those deeper layers.

Once you can mindfully allow the fight state to be there, you can act on the impulses within it. When you feel into that fight energy, you may notice an impulse about what to do next. Your body may know what it wants to do with it. If you can mindfully experience that, you may notice some polyvagal shifts start to happen, and some ladder climbing along with it.
You have to be able to mindfully listen to your body and experience the sensations underneath the emotion of anger. If you can do that, it will tell you what to do next. An impulse will arise.

With anger, it's probably going to involve the upper body: throwing, squeezing, pushing, hitting. Those are just examples. I don't encourage you to do any of these things to anybody. In fact, I'm telling you, don't do that. That's not a good idea. And again, you shouldn't be doing any of this unless you have the distress tolerance for it.

When you act on these impulses mindlessly, you may end up harming somebody, harming yourself, or destroying something. When you act on them mindfully, you can actually enable some ladder climbing. If the impulse is to squeeze, you can squeeze a fidget, or some clothing, or a towel, or a paper towel roll. I think the paper towel roll was a Peter Levine example: grabbing one and squeezing it. That's a way to mindfully experience and use the impulse without harming yourself or anybody else, and ladder climbing can happen from there.

blocks.h: Why I don't start with the thoughts

blocks.p: I don't recommend simply trying to combat the angry thoughts. I don't think thought replacement is very easy, especially on your own. In therapy, it's totally doable, because you have someone there to co-regulate with you, someone who can validate first and then offer a cognitive reframe.

On your own, trying to combat your thoughts and change your thinking is very difficult and very frustrating, and it probably feeds right back into the anger and the fight state. You may end up berating yourself, judging yourself, shaming yourself, blaming yourself. It becomes more aggressive thinking on top of the aggressive thinking that was already there, and it just reinforces the anger and the fight state, mindlessly.

Instead, focus on the emotion driving those thoughts, then go a bit deeper and eventually experience the sensations underneath. From those sensations, an impulse may arise that you can mindfully act on.
So there are a few options for dealing with anger:

ol: Address the thoughts directly. Possible, but hard on your own, and it can feed the anger.
Address the emotion, sensations, and impulses underneath the thoughts. Allow the fight state, feel into it, and mindfully act on the impulse that arises.
Leave those where they are and anchor in safety instead.

blocks.p: If you can't address the thoughts directly, and you can't address the emotion and sensations underneath them either, because that's also very challenging, the third option is to anchor in safety. Don't address the thoughts or the anger directly unless you can handle it. Instead, you might say to your anger:

"I know you're there. I feel you. You've made yourself obvious, and I'm going to let you hang out with me. While you hang out in my little pocket over here, I'm also going to do something that is very anchoring for me, something where I feel some measure of safety or groundedness."

It's not about rejecting your feelings. They're there anyway, so let them be there, and also do something that anchors you in your safety state. If you can do that, you might notice the intensity of the anger softens, and the intensity of the angry thoughts softens too. If you can anchor yourself really effectively, the anger and the angry thoughts may eventually not be an issue at all.
I hope this acts as a reframe for your anger, and for how to "deal with it."

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.
